items.title: Bloomberg: "To be fair, the trade in physical goods hasn’t expanded as fast as the overall global economy over the past decade, which means it isn’t...
items.description_html:
Bloomberg: "To be fair, the trade in physical goods hasn’t expanded as fast as the overall global economy over the past decade, which means it isn’t the engine it once was. But neither has it collapsed. And the World Trade Organization this week said it actually expected that, at 3.9% this year, trade would again grow faster than global GDP."

Could we be misunderstanding the data? After all, while both the US deficit and Chinese surplus have continued to grow, the US deficit with China has dropped sharply, which suggests that what used to show up in the data as $100 trade between China and the US may now show up in the data as $200-300 of trade as the goods are intermediated through various countries. In that case is trade really growing nearly as fast as the growth in trade data?
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-09/trump-brexit-and-tariffs-haven-t-stopped-globalization?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter

FT: "China’s growing debt pile is constraining the government’s fiscal capacity for sweeping new stimulus to revive flagging domestic demand and strengthen economic growth, studies of state finances show."

Although you probably wouldn't know this from reading the Chinese or foreign press, China probably has the worst debt dynamics of any major economy today. Its debt-to-GDP ratio is the second highest (after Japan) and is the fastest growing in history.

items.title: NYT: "Maros Sefcovic, the trade commissioner of the 27-nation bloc, said that the understanding could lead to China’s halving the number of hybrid ga...
items.description_html:
NYT: "Maros Sefcovic, the trade commissioner of the 27-nation bloc, said that the understanding could lead to China’s halving the number of hybrid gasoline-electric cars that it sends to the European Union in the next four years."

This may seem like a victory, but the problem is a systemic one, and not sectoral. Because this agreement does not in any way address either China's demand imbalance or the overall role of the EU in absorbing that imbalance, it won't have much effect on overall EU manufacturing. All that will happen is a shift in the locus of net manufacturing imports from China, so that EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers.

For historical reasons, trade discussions are usually held on a product-by-product basis, but while that may make sense in a world of broadly balanced trade, it makes no sense in a world of deep, persistent imbalances. China runs huge surpluses not because it produces too many hybrids but rather because of its deep consumption imbalance and the very low household income share of GDP.

As long as that happens, the only recourse for the EU, if it does not want to accept deindustrialization, is either to reduce its own household share of GDP (which would be politically disruptive as well as bad for the global economy) or to intervene in its external accounts in such a way that it reverses the competitive impact of China's low household share of GDP.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/china-european-union-trade.html?smid=tw-share

items.title: FT: “China has rejected an EU request to voluntarily restrict its surging exports of hybrid cars to the bloc as the two sides enter last-ditch talks ...
items.description_html:
FT: “China has rejected an EU request to voluntarily restrict its surging exports of hybrid cars to the bloc as the two sides enter last-ditch talks to avert a trade conflict.”

While this may be bad news for the EU auto industry, it doesn’t matter much to overall EU manufacturing sectors. Voluntary restraints can reduce China’s trade surplus in autos, but because they have no impact on China’s underlying imbalances, they can’t have much impact on China’s overall manufacturing surplus with the EU.

To the extent that voluntary restraints on Chinese auto exports to the EU would have benefitted EU auto producers, in other words, the benefits would have come at the expense of other EU manufacturers.

This does show, however, just how difficult it is for China to rebalance its economy and how dependent Chinese manufacturers are on foreign demand. Beijing has very little room to accommodate even relatively mild foreign needs.
https://www.ft.com/content/32e1c801-fe7d-4389-b3fc-ab687cbb087b via @ft

items.title: Very interesting paper on the relationship between imports and household debt in the US. Note the conclusion: "We show that household debt increases s...
items.description_html:
Very interesting paper on the relationship between imports and household debt in the US. Note the conclusion: "We show that household debt increases significantly in regions in which manufacturing industries are more exposed to import competition."

American economists usually argue that it is the prior decision by American households to borrow and spend that causes the US to run a trade deficit. This study suggests causality may run in the other direction, so that those areas most affected by net imports are precisely where household debt is most likely to rise.

Of course the accounting identity itself says either can be true.

items.title: This article indirectly describes one of the more important consequences of our current, distorted form of globalization, even if it isn't commented u...
items.description_html:
This article indirectly describes one of the more important consequences of our current, distorted form of globalization, even if it isn't commented upon enough. Automation will help Japanese and Korean shipbuilders compete with Chinese shipbuilders only if wages don't rise in line with productivity.

In a system in which nations "win" at manufacturing mainly by suppressing unit labor costs, every country that wants a large manufacturing sector is under pressure either to suppress household income (including by reducing transfers) or to raise productivity without allowing a commensurate rise in wages.

This is the kind of world Keynes warned about, in which countries try to expand production while suppressing demand.

But while a few individual countries can get away with beggar-thy-neighbor growth policies, the world itself cannot do so. If too many countries try to suppress wages, or expand productivity while suppressing the accompanying wage growth, the only way to keep demand and supply balanced globally is with surging debt.

It is of course a good thing if businesses and governments around the world invest to expand productivity growth, but it is not a good thing if workers' wages don't rise in line with the growth in productivity. There's no point in making more stuff if people can't afford to buy it.

This is why Joan Robinson warned that the inevitable result of beggar-thy-neighbor policies, once deficit countries are no longer able politically to bear the costs, is a breakdown in trade. Rising debt and suppressed wages can only go on for so long.
https://www.ft.com/content/ea32c53d-4de7-4b34-af44-cc148b23433f via @ft

items.description_html:
RT Indian Express Hindi
10 अक्टूबर को दिल्ली में हुए प्रदर्शन को कवर करने के लिए इंडियन एक्सप्रेस हिंदी की टीम ग्राउंड पर मौजूद थी. शाम को लगभग 6 बजे, कवरेज के दौरान विजय और स्वाति की टीम की बातचीत एक पुलिस अधिकारी से हुई. उनके कंधे पर तीन स्टार थे और उन्होंने क्रिकेट के खेल में इस्तेमाल होने वाला हेल्मेट पहना हुआ था.

विजय से बातचीत के दौरान उन्होंने ऐसा दर्शाया कि वो विजय को पहले से जानते थे. विजय ने मना कर दिया. पुलिस अधिकारी ने बातचीत जारी रखी.

इतने में हमारा ध्यान उनके चश्मे पर गया. मालूम पड़ा कि उन्होंने रेबैन के मेटा ग्लासेज़ पहने हुए थे. वो शायद रिकॉर्डिंग भी कर रहे थे. सवाल पूछने पर अधिकारी ने कहा कि वो रिकॉर्डिंग नहीं कर रहे थे.

हमने अपनी फ़ुटेज चेक की तो पाया कि उसी पुलिस अधिकारी की तस्वीरें हमारे कैमरे में कैद हुई थीं. हम वो तस्वीर यहां दिखा रहे हैं.

सवाल ये हैं:
क्या पुलिसकर्मियों को निगरानी रखने या किसी भी और इरादे से, ये स्मार्ट चश्मे दिए गए हैं?
यदि हां, तो क्यों?
यदि नहीं, तो क्या कोई पुलिसकर्मी, ड्यूटी के दौरान, ऐसे स्मार्ट चश्मे पहन सकता है? और लोगों की अनधिकृत रिकॉर्डिंग कर सकता है?

India is adding renewable capacity faster than it can move the power. The bottleneck is not the solar parks or modules now its now everything around transmitting that power to your homes

GEC-II : strengthening intra-state transmission in RE-rich states to evacuate ~20 GW

GEC-III (proposed) : being evaluated to integrate ~135 GW of renewables + 25 GW of pumped storage

Thats nearly 7x the RE scale.

More GW > more lines > more substations > more transformers > more grid equipment

This can drive a multi year T&D cycle

items.title: When everyone is buying the “hot theme”, what should you be doing? India has seen a new market darling almost every year. The problem? By the time a...
items.description_html:
When everyone is buying the “hot theme”, what should you be doing?

India has seen a new market darling almost every year.
The problem? By the time a theme becomes popular, a large part of the compounding may already be behind you.

A fascinating study by Persistence Capital looked at 16 major themes from 2015–2023.

The finding: 13 out of 16 themes underperformed the NSE 500 three years after becoming popular.
The first year often looked great. The trouble came later.

The deck goes theme-by-theme, analysing what investors believed at the time vs. what actually happened.

A great exercise in “invert, always invert.”

Before asking “What’s working right now?” ask: “What usually happens to people who chase what’s already working?”

𑁍 Read the full deck: https://docsend.com/view/g3vkigu8v8inugkp

Worth 20 minutes for anyone who has ever felt the temptation to chase the hottest theme.

Keep learning, keep compounding.

items.title: ₹104 lakh crore. That's the combined market cap of the 15 largest companies in the Nifty 50. Over the last three years, the median company in this gr...
items.description_html:
₹104 lakh crore. That's the combined market cap of the 15 largest companies in the Nifty 50. Over the last three years, the median company in this group grew EPS at 14.7% a year.

Reliance, HDFC Bank, TCS, Infosys and Kotak make up 41% of this basket. Their 3Y EPS CAGR is 6% to 10%, at or below India's nominal GDP growth

In most of the names there have been broad based PE derating event that has taken place

But why is it happening?

A. The starting point. Five years ago was peak liquidity, and many of these names entered this period at multiples that already priced in a decade of growth

B. Growth leadership changed hands. IT is wrestling with the AI-disruption question, FMCG is watching growth leak to D2C and quick commerce, HDFC Bank spent these years digesting a mega-merger, and Reliance's earnings still lean on a cyclical O2C core.

One should ask oneself what the driver of growth in the economy is and are those drivers of growth present in the Index?

C. The natural owners left. FPIs sold 1.66 lakh crore of Indian equities in 2025 and roughly 2.4 lakh crore more in 2026 so far. FPI ownership fell to 14.7% in May, a 14-year low.

But one should understand this that money isn't leaving India. It's leaving the index.

SIPs hit a record 32,297 crore in August. Same month, large-cap funds saw net outflows of 1,147 crore while small-cap (7,973 cr) and mid-cap (6,989 cr) funds took the biggest inflows

Even FPIs, while selling on the exchanges, kept writing cheques in the IPO market

Why? Because the themes driving this market barely live in the index: power and T&D equipment, defence, electronics manufacturing, capital-market infrastructure, hospitals, data centres, CDMOs. India's capex and formalisation cycle is being built by mid caps, recent listings and companies that are a sliver of Nifty 50 weight

The index has stopped being the default answer. This is a stock picker's market, company by company, inside the Nifty and far beyond it.

The Nifty tells you where India made its money. It no longer tells you where India will make it next.

Disclaimer - This is only for educational purposes and not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.title: RT Nandakishor m: Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sou...
items.description_html:
RT Nandakishor m
Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome
Blog: https://www.nandakishorm.com/writing/vega
GitHub: https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/vegaml

items.title: Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily...
items.description_html:
Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily connects a phone, vehical or a device to the network. ISAC turns telco infra into a wide area sensing network to detect, tract objects, including drones without needing a dedicated radar at every sensing location. This is such a critical part of the security sovereignty. For existing telcos, this means, theycan offer sensing services using same infra. A potential new revenue stream.

In AI native physical world, radio networks could become sources of realtime information about moving objects & their surroundings. Combine this with AI, you can support traffic optimization, industrial monitoring, infra/public protection.

If India can develop, deploy sophisticated sensing enabled telco infra, we gain the capabilities that go beyond simply buying connectivity from a foreign stellite provider who can cut us off in ever changing geopolitical situation.

Eventually, everything is down to who controls the network and the data? Market access cannot be isolated from national security. It's all about who gets a strategic control over the next layer of digital infra.

items.title: RT Prasanna Tantri: To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chok...
items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Tantri
To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chokepoints. It shows how America turned its dominance in finance and technology into instruments of state policy.

Private ownership offers no insulation from state power. The restrictions on Huawei and ZTE illustrate how dependence on American technology can become a source of geopolitical vulnerability. Under the Foreign Direct Product Rule, even companies outside America needed US permission to supply Huawei with certain products made using American technology. Washington’s reach extended far beyond American firms and borders.

India should take that lesson seriously. Greater dependence on foreign-controlled critical infrastructure creates the risk that commercial access will eventually become conditional on political compliance.

Economic interdependence can deliver prosperity. But in periods of geopolitical conflict, it can also constrain a country’s freedom to make its own choices. Short-term commercial gains must be weighed against that loss of autonomy.

India is right to insist on security safeguards for Starlink. Economic sovereignty is difficult to recover once critical dependencies are entrenched.

items.title: For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase ...
items.description_html:
For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase we're in. The reasoning is on the way to getting commodatized. For in infra player, cost are insanely high & capex is forever. What they sell out in market *was* getting premium. It's temporal. The time to be bullish on infra was late 2023, early 2024.

When people say AI is in bubble, it's the infra players & their stock prices not the rest of the part of the value chain.

In the last two decades, we saw similar cycles playing out with specialized server builders. The value went out and accrued in software.

There are two way forward. For an LLM OEM, raising prices will not work. The only other way is build around the reasoning. Build tools, harness, something valuable that keeps enterprises spending. There is no clear path to profitability for these LLM players & the IPOs are looking to suck everything out. The value will once again move out and get into data, harness, security, the non infra part. With non programmers vibe coding & putting millions of lines of code, agents into production, diff set of value pockets attracts premium. The infra players who build tools for observability, auditability, monitoring, governance will still stay very relevant.

I read it long ago that in market cycles, themes pick up & initially few believe in it. Eventually, everyone starts believing in it. In my view with infra, we're in this phase. Demand won't go down, but premium won't be same. The early investors of infra have moved deep within value chain, away from infra if you track deals globally. Then the open weight models, onchip inference and so much architectural advancements awaiting in line. The transition will be much faster, if not instant.

items.title: Small Company, Big Signal: Vikram Thermo at CPHI Milan 2026 Vikram Thermo is a small Indian manufacturer of pharmaceutical coating polymers competing ...
items.description_html:
Small Company, Big Signal: Vikram Thermo at CPHI Milan 2026

Vikram Thermo is a small Indian manufacturer of pharmaceutical coating polymers competing against much larger global excipient suppliers.

At CPHI Milan, it made a statement. A prominent concourse hoarding read: “Never the headline, always the reason.” Its booth carried another message: “Innovation in every layer.”

What would Robert M. Grant make of this?

The company's moat is unlikely to be its brand. It is the cost of replacing an approved polymer in an established formulation, the accumulated technical knowledge of customer-specific applications, and the trust built through years of consistent performance.

The interesting question is whether Vikram Thermo can turn that trust into a broader competitive advantage.

The branding signals ambition. The R&D push could be more consequential. Better technical capabilities can deepen existing relationships, open new formulation opportunities and move the company beyond supplying equivalent grades.

But the sequence matters. Branding can attract attention. Only capability can sustain it.

Three things are worth watching: whether visibility generates new formulation trials, whether proprietary grades become a meaningful revenue contributor, and whether technical expertise becomes embedded in organisational routines rather than remaining dependent on a few individuals.

A small company does not need to match the scale of global competitors. It needs to become difficult to replace.

The signal is encouraging. The evidence will be in the customer wins, the product pipeline and the economics that follow.

Disclosure: I have been invested in Vikram Thermo since 2020 and intend to remain invested for the very long term, provided the balance sheet remains clean and lean and the company continues to execute on its innovation-led ambitions. This reflects my current assessment and is subject to change as evidence evolves.

This is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold the stock.

The smartest conversations aren’t about finding out what a company plans to do this year or next. They’re about exchanging perspectives, challenging assumptions, and understanding where the industry is heading.

When you shift the conversation from individual business interests to the broader industry, people share more openly, perspectives become richer, and insights emerge that you won’t find in any presentation or report.

That’s where the real gold lies!

items.title: RT Swapnil Srivastav: 🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame. Here’s ...
items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: US telecom stocks crashed up to 13–14% on Friday. European telecom stocks also fell 4–5%, as investors saw Elon Musk as a growing threat in that reg...
items.description_html:
US telecom stocks crashed up to 13–14% on Friday. European telecom stocks also fell 4–5%, as investors saw Elon Musk as a growing threat in that region too.

🚨How India reacts to Reliance (Jio) and Airtel will be seen on Monday!!

- On Friday, Oct 9, Elon Musk announced that SpaceX agreed to buy a nationwide block of low-band spectrum (800 MHz) from Grain Management for reported $8 billion.

- Low-band spectrum travels farther and goes through walls/buildings/cities better.

- Combined with Starlink’s satellites (and recent approval for 15,000 more), this lets Starlink Mobile build a hybrid satellite + ground network.

- With his SpaceX will become a major full mobile carrier in the US with better coverage, including indoors.

- Musk called it the “last critical piece” and a “very big deal.” He also described it as an “earthquake” in the spectrum world.

🚨Why US telecom stocks crashed?

- Traditional carriers (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile) depend on expensive towers and spectrum.

- Investors feared a cash-rich SpaceX could now compete more directly and take customers or force price cuts.

- On Friday, T-Mobile down ~13%, AT&T and Verizon down ~9–10% , some of their worst days in years.

Why Europe markets also reacted:

- Same fear: Starlink’s expanding direct-to-phone capability could eventually challenge European carriers too.

- Stocks of Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, Orange and others dropped 4–8%.

🚨Why this is a threat to Indian Telecom players like Airtel and Jio

- For Musk, India is the most lucrative large market after the US, making players like Jio and Airtel's duopoly vulnerable.

- SpaceX is sitting on a lot of cash and can move aggressively once clearances come, including his disruption and price warfare.

- Jio and Airtel dominate India’s market and have spent heavily on towers and spectrum.

- Starlink already has a licence and partnerships with them for rural areas, but full launch is still pending security and spectrum clearances.

- A working Starlink Mobile in the US proves the model works and raises the risk that Musk can disrupt pricing, coverage and the traditional tower model in India too.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight

Saudi Arabia’s crude supply fell to its lowest level in more than three decades in August, at roughly 6 million barrels per day

Supply conditions remain constrained in September, while Saudi Aramco has now halted October crude deliveries to at least two European refiners following renewed disruptions to its critical East-West pipeline

Earlier in the year, Saudi Arabia increasingly relied on the East-West pipeline to bypass disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, helping keep more crude flowing to global markets

That alternative route has now itself been disrupted following a series of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure

Despite this increasingly difficult macro backdrop, markets have remained remarkably resilient

But beneath the surface, participation continues to weaken
Most stocks have recovered even as broader market breadth continues to deteriorate

A lot is riding on Q2FY27 earnings

Wont be too aggressive in building new positions, nor too aggressive in booking existing ones

items.title: RT Kunal Kapoor: Watching Elon Musk this week has been a fascinating character study in the saviour complex of Western tech billionaires. They arrive ...
items.description_html:
RT Kunal Kapoor
Watching Elon Musk this week has been a fascinating character study in the saviour complex of Western tech billionaires.

They arrive in your country selling you the future. Welcome them, and you’re a country that wants progress. Make them wait, and suddenly your people are victims who need rescuing from their own institutions by the chosen one.

It’s a pattern. When Thai rescuers didn’t use the mini-submarine Musk sent for the trapped boys, and diver Vernon Unsworth called the idea impractical, Musk attacked him as the “pedo guy.”

When Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered X to comply with its rulings, Musk called the judge a “dictator.”

The script rarely changes. Only the country does.

The colonial mindset isn’t always about wanting to rule a country. Sometimes it’s the assumption that you arrive as its saviour, and if the country doesn’t immediately recognise you as one, something must be wrong with the country.

items.title: RT Ananth Rupanagudi: 1855, the Cotton Ground and market, Colaba, Bombay. Colaba’s cotton ground and market history transformed Bombay (now Mumbai) f...
items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
1855, the Cotton Ground and market, Colaba, Bombay. Colaba’s cotton ground and market history transformed Bombay (now Mumbai) from a cluster of islands into a global financial and trade hub.

In the 17th and early 18th centuries, Bombay Green (near present-day Horniman Circle) served as the city's primary open-air market where merchants auctioned raw cotton bales. As cotton exports surged—accelerated by global demand—Bombay Green became too congested and prone to fires. The wholesale cotton market shifted south to a spacious meadow in Colaba beside the harbour, establishing the New Cotton Green.

The opening of the Cotton Exchange in Colaba in 1844 solidified the area as a cornerstone of maritime commerce, aided by the completion of the Colaba Causeway in 1838 which connected the southern islands.

However, it shifted permanently from Colaba to the Sewri-Mazgaon reclamation area in central-eastern Mumbai during the early 20th century. The present-day Cotton Green railway station on the Harbour Line stands as a reminder of this final relocation.

The decision to move the massive trading operations out of Colaba was driven by infrastructural challenges and the rapid industrial evolution of Bombay. Factors like massive congestion and space constraints, especially during the boom period of the American Civil war, the threat of fire hazards, and the requirement of the land for the expansion of the port were the primary factors for shifting the market out of Colaba.

By the early 1900s, Mumbai's textile manufacturing center had moved north into areas like Parel, Lalbaug, and Worli (collectively known as Girangaon or the village of mills). Moving the raw cotton market to Sewri placed the supply much closer to the actual spinning and weaving mills. #Mumbai #cotton #history @mumbaiheritage @dhavalkulkarni @SachinKalbag

items.title: RT Joshua Saxe: Reaction to the @slatestarcodex vs. @sapinker AI x-risk debate The main problem with this debate is that both interlocutors are mainly...
items.description_html:
RT Joshua Saxe
Reaction to the @slatestarcodex vs. @sapinker AI x-risk debate

The main problem with this debate is that both interlocutors are mainly focused on AI as a disembodied technological object that's fallen down from heaven, not a congealed mass of human decisions.

Scott has understood that there's nothing ontological about deep learning that'd prevent us from killing ourselves with it and that this risk gets worse as AI scales. But this is a trivial observation!

Here's how to kill everyone with AI: put Opus 8.1-Killeveryone in charge of 100 bio labs; skimp on safety post-training; connect it to the Internet; let it develop affective relationships with the lab post-docs and its nihilist friends on Reddit; don't monitor it; have it work as a swarm to solve 'BioKillEveryoneGym' over a holiday break...

In fairness, Pinker and Alexander do touch on social processes. But if one is concerned with scenarios like these, 90% of the debate should focus on the social processes by which we risk creating them - incentives, culture, guardrails, ... - and on why we won't adapt and reach a reasonable equilibrium somewhere along the way.

To be clear, I'm very concerned about AI harms - including tail harms - but not very concerned about extinction risks. The burden is on Pinker and deep learning denialists to show that AI couldn't kill everyone under any circumstances (hard to defend); but the burden is on Alexander to show the social mechanisms by which we’d make the long sequence of low-probability unforced errors that would actually allow it to do this (seems hard to defend).

We could kill a lot of people with nuclear power plants. Here's how: don't monitor them. Fire all their safety engineers. Build them in the middle of all of the world's population centers and then cut off their water supplies whenever city budgets run low.

That we haven't done this is heartening; we should understand why. That there've been many accidents with dangerous technologies, especially in the earlier phases as we thrash towards a safety equilibrium, is disheartening; we should understand why those happened, too, and apply all those lessons to AI.

items.description_html:
RT Sustainable Futures Collaborative
As India advances towards the more ambitious and hard-to-attain 500 GW non-fossil domestic target by 2030, the central challenge is no longer merely the scale of non-fossil capacity deployment. Rather, it lies in ensuring that this capacity is effectively integrated into the power system and translated into actual clean electricity generation that delivers broad socioeconomic benefits. In other words, capacity deployment should simultaneously pave the way for system integration and socioeconomic transformation.

In @Ideas4India, @SaradaPD and Shubhranshu Suman explain why we need to think beyond capacity addition amid a growing and increasingly volatile electricity demand. They argue that policy attention must shift towards increasing the share of electricity generated from non-fossil sources, better integrating renewables into the grid, and fostering productive use of power that can generate livelihood opportunities.

items.title: RT Deedy: The smartest Indians continue to come to build in the US for the simple reason that the economic incentives are far far better. Perplexity (...
items.description_html:
RT Deedy
The smartest Indians continue to come to build in the US for the simple reason that the economic incentives are far far better.

Perplexity ($20B), Skild ($14B+), Baseten ($13B), Together ($8B), Glean ($8B), Modal ($5B), Rubrik ($25B), Harness ($5B), Blacksmith, Parallel, Greptile, CodeRabbit, Composio, Distyl ($2B), Resolve, Luma, Cartesia, Wispr, dMatrix, Arize and many more - all started by at least one Indian-born founder.

The US is a far easier to raise capital in with far less dilution. Most Indian companies are switching where they're domiciled to get access to the US capital markets. Every single Indian venture firm is trying very hard to invest in the US or risk not participating in the AI race (ironically, the management fees of venture firms are so high in India relatively that this is the one group that net of carry actually has incentive to be in India because they take home well north of a living wage whether or not funds perform do)

While Zomato ($35B now, $8B at IPO) might be the biggest outcome in Indian venture, Cursor ($60B), Reflection (potentially $20B+), World Labs ($8B), OpenRouter ($8B), HuggingFace ($12B) and of course the $1T+ big labs quickly make those outcomes seem small and happen on a much smaller time scale, with much higher IRR.

Engineers at these startups regularly get paid $1M/yr, and make $10M+ on exit. Even in BigTech, it is trivial to pull up levels fyi and see that if you're L6/L7+ with ~10 years of experience, you're making $1M/yr there too. And of course, we all know the slew of Indian CEOs of companies here, not to mention a huge bench of lesser known executives across the board in public and private companies.

I say all this because every time there is a slight immigration hiccup in the US, I hear the online pleas to "build in India", I struggle to understand why most engineers, academics or founders would do that net of desire to be close to family, failure to obtain visa and devout patriotism.

This is not a superiority thing or a US v India thing. The economic incentives at least for technologists to being in the US outweigh India by at least an order of magnitude.

Temple freedom is often discussed as important for the organisation of Hindu society. Yet there is little research to inform this debate, largely because few such institutions in India can be studied at scale.

I took this up in my PhD in Economics at the University of Cambridge. I examined how Hindu mutts, among the few Hindu institutions to have retained significant institutional autonomy at scale, have contributed to human capital formation and driven positive structural transformation in the communities they serve.

In this podcast, I discuss my research with @srajagopalan of the Mercatus Center at George Mason University on @IdeasofIndia. Thank you, Shruti, for being a fantastic host and for a wonderful conversation.

We also discuss interesting examples of autonomous religious institutions around the world. I share how Hindu mutts, being outside state control, have served as engines of social and economic progress.

News🗞️ The US has suspended major IT firms including TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant from the PERM programme, amid a broader investigation into alleged H-1B and immigration programme abuse.

PERM is a key step in the employment-based green card process.

Interestingly, PERM filings by some of these Indian IT majors had already fallen sharply. TCS and Wipro reported zero filings in 2025, while Infosys was also at negligible/zero levels depending on the filing dataset.

So while the headline is negative, the immediate financial impact may be more limited than it first appears.

Bigger concern is whether this marks the start of a wider US crackdown on the Indian IT outsourcing model 🤔

items.description_html:
RT Capitalmind Mutual Fund
Sector Leadership Map - October 2026

Key sectors weakened over the past month. Here's what the data says.

Our Sector Leadership Map looks at two things: how each sector performed relative to the Nifty 500 and how many of its stocks are trading above their 200-day moving average.

The hollow dots show where each sector was a month ago. The filled dots show where they are today. And the line connecting these dots shows how they moved.

Pharma is the standout. It outperformed the Nifty 500 by 5% and around 65% of its stocks remain above the 200 DMA.

On the other hand, Metals saw one of the sharpest reversals. A month ago it was comfortably outperforming with around 85% of its stocks above the 200DMA. Today, it is underperforming and breadth has fallen to 43%.

FMCG moved the other way on relative returns. It went from underperforming the Nifty 500 by nearly 6% to outperforming by about 3%. But breadth fell from 27% to just 7%.

So while some sector indices have held up better than others, participation underneath them has weakened almost everywhere.

The panel explored how sovereign ratings must evolve in an increasingly fragmented global environment and how emerging markets can attract capital through stronger institutions, credible reforms and predictable policy and regulatory frameworks.

The conversation also examined India’s resilience amid global geopolitical and fiscal uncertainty. The panellists highlighted how India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, reform momentum, demographic advantages and improving ease of doing business continue to reinforce its position as an attractive global investment destination.

A key theme was the need to mobilise private capital for infrastructure and development through innovative financing structures, including blended finance, guarantees, securitisation and sustainable finance instruments. The discussion emphasised the importance of policy stability, institutional credibility and financial innovation in supporting long-term economic growth.

The panel also highlighted the considerable potential of emerging markets, including economies across Africa, and the need for balanced assessment frameworks that recognise opportunities, strategic importance and reform progress alongside prevailing risks and vulnerabilities.

The conversation underscored the opportunity for India and GIFT City to emerge as major global financial hubs by deepening capital markets, expanding financial products and leveraging India’s strengths in technology, analytics and financial services.

Despite an uncertain global environment, the panel reaffirmed confidence in India’s long-term growth trajectory and GIFT City’s potential to serve as an international gateway for global capital.

At its second anniversary celebrations, #CareEdgeGlobal launched its latest report, “A Case for Reforms: Building Sovereign Resilience in an Evolving World.”

The report assesses 43 reform cases across 38 countries through two complementary matrices. The first maps reforms across the five pillars of CareEdge Global Ratings’ sovereign rating methodology, while the second examines them through a geographic lens.

The study covers 12 reforms from the Americas, 11 each from APAC and Europe, and nine from Africa. These include 14 fiscal, eight economic, eight external, seven monetary, and six institutional reforms.

Of the cases assessed, 15 are classified as Work in Progress, 10 as Highly Effective, and nine each as Moderately Effective and Least Effective.
Drawing on reform experiences across regions and policy areas, the report offers valuable insights into the factors that shape reform effectiveness and highlights how credible implementation can strengthen sovereign resilience and support credit quality in an evolving global environment.

items.title: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, sparing the US refining capacity of a direct hit. The main refineries alongside his path were >15...
items.description_html:
Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, sparing the US refining capacity of a direct hit. The main refineries alongside his path were >150km away in Mobile (AL) and Pascagoula (MS). Refined fuel production (and offshore crude production) should recover quickly.


Javier Blas: The first hurricane of the North Atlantic season: Isais, which has formed inside the US Gulf of Mexico. On current tracking forecast, the threat is limited to GoM oil production. Crucially, little refining capacity in Alabama (3 refineries in total, with ~140,000 of capacity).

items.description_html:
RT Special Envoy Steve Witkoff
Today, representatives from the United States, the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO met in Miami and held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace.

The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession.

The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia. Participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to continuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable peace that strengthens security and creates opportunities for lasting stability and prosperity.

items.title: RT Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський: Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were...
items.description_html:
RT Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський
Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill, there must be support for Ukraine in protecting lives, and there must be pressure on Russia for its war. And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different.

Recently, there was a European decision to lift sanctions on Russian oligarchs. Since then, Russian strikes and the torment of people have only increased. This past week alone, there was a brutal Russian missile strike on a residential building in Pryluky, aerial bombs were dropped on Kramatorsk – on ordinary city buses – and there have been constant attacks on Kyiv’s energy infrastructure and on the life-sustaining infrastructure in Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, and our other cities. Dozens of people have been killed and hundreds wounded.

The Russians are compensating for their inability to achieve their objectives on the battlefield with this kind of terror. This year, Russia is weaker on the battlefield than at any other point in the war. That is why Putin is relying on terror. That is why he is relying on attempts to strike backroom deals to secure some form of pressure relief for Russia, in order to buy more time and more opportunities for war.

Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness. It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world.

Ukraine is ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps, and the American team knows our position. Our strikes on Russian oil refineries and other oil facilities are a response to Russia’s years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy sector. Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the United States has enough power to achieve such a compromise.

Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will “repay” the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis.

We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one.

Retail leads all sectors with 66,557 announcements so far in 2026, followed by Technology, at 22,361, and Aerospace and Defense, at 21,841.

Hiring demand remains muted.

items.description_html:
China’s industrial profit growth is losing momentum:

China’s industrial profits rose +4.2% YoY in August, the weakest YoY growth since November 2025.

This also marks the 4th consecutive monthly slowdown in growth.

Pressure is particularly visible in consumer-facing industries, where profits are falling in autos, clothing, and furniture.

Domestic demand continues to weaken, with consumption growth slowing to near zero while manufacturers, property developers, and infrastructure builders are cutting spending.

For the first 8 months of 2026, industrial profits were still up +15.7% YoY, but the gains are becoming increasingly concentrated, with the electronics industry contributing ~66% of total growth.

At the same time, raw-material industries contributed +6.2 percentage points to the overall increase, supported by higher commodity prices.

Weak domestic demand is weighing on China’s economy.

items.title: The US deficit is surging despite low unemployment. The cumulative US fiscal deficit since 2020 has surged to a massive $14.18 trillion. Meanwhile, th...
items.description_html:
The US deficit is surging despite low unemployment.

The cumulative US fiscal deficit since 2020 has surged to a massive $14.18 trillion.

Meanwhile, the 7-year average unemployment rate has fallen -0.4 percentage points, to 4.7% over the same period.

In the first 11 months of FY2026 alone, the US deficit totaled $1.97 trillion, the 3rd-largest for this period of the year in history.

When the economy is strong and unemployment is low, the government would typically keep fiscal deficits lower, reserving large-scale fiscal support for periods of economic weakness.

This time, however, the deficit is running at historically high levels despite stable unemployment.

This comes as elevated government spending and rising interest costs are keeping the deficit exceptionally large even without a recession.

Massive deficits have become a permanent feature of the US economy.

items.title: Shocking stat of the day: $241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds. This figure is up...
items.description_html:
Shocking stat of the day:

$241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds.

This figure is up +1,621% from just $14 billion at the start of 2026.

This means ~38% of French high-grade corporate debt is now trading at lower yields than government bonds of similar maturity.

The gap between corporate and government bond yields is widening as investor concerns about France's deteriorating fiscal situation weigh on government debt.

As a result, internationally exposed companies such as L'Oreal, $OR, and TotalEnergies, $TTE, are increasingly viewed as safer alternatives to French government debt, unlike French banks, which remain more exposed to sovereign risk.

This is in stark contrast to normal economic conditions, when government bonds are traditionally viewed as the safest part of the bond market.

France's corporate bond market is increasingly being treated a safer bet than its government bonds.

items.title: Breaking News ! RBI comes in big with measures to defend the Rupee ! PS: I have been saying every day since the RBI policy last week, that the Rupee p...
items.description_html:
Breaking News !

RBI comes in big with measures to defend the Rupee !

PS: I have been saying every day since the RBI policy last week, that the Rupee problem needs to be addressed.

Here is what RBI has announced,

1. The RBI is taking the PSU oil companies’ dollar demand directly onto its own book. From Oct-12, the RBI will supply the full daily dollar requirement of IOC, HPCL & BPCL via designated banks. Basically - these large, regular dollar buyers do not have to come into the market everyday & push up demand for dollars.

2. Large USD-buying hedges will now cost banks more. For certain INR derivative trades above $2 million, banks must keep 20% of the Rupee value in cash with the RBI as a reserve. That makes these trades more expensive.

3. The amount you can trade without proving you actually have an underlying FX need has been slashed. The limit has gone from $100 million to just $5 million. This applies both to OTC derivatives & exchange-traded currency derivatives.

4. You can’t cancel a Rupee FX trade & then simply put the same trade back on again ! Rollovers at maturity are still allowed. Basically meant to curb repeated trading around the same exposure.

5. You now have to certify that you haven’t hedged the same exposure somewhere else. Bascially the RBI is trying to stop the same $ requirement being used to justify multiple hedges.

items.title: RT Prashant Nair: The Rupee problem ! The RBI has turned more hawkish, but the question is whether it has moved enough. A 25 bps hike & tougher langua...
items.description_html:
RT Prashant Nair
The Rupee problem !

The RBI has turned more hawkish, but the question is whether it has moved enough.

A 25 bps hike & tougher language may buy some support for the Rupee, but if the market believes the RBI will continue moving cautiously (2/6 voted against change in stance) - that support may not last. The risk is that the market keeps testing the currency until policy becomes sufficiently restrictive.

Unless Oil falls sharply, the burden to defend the Rupee increasingly shifts to interest rates. There is also the RBI’s large forward book. That has helped contain near-term pressure on the Rupee, but it leaves a substantial overhang. Given its size, normalising that position could take years !

#Rupee #Nifty #BankNifty #Investing #RBI

items.title: RT Nimesh Shah: Brokearges on RBI Measures CITI RBI announced FX measures that tighten derivative rules by restricting cancelled contract rebooking, l...
items.description_html:
RT Nimesh Shah
Brokearges on RBI Measures
CITI
RBI announced FX measures that tighten derivative rules by restricting cancelled contract rebooking, lowering unhedged threshold to $5mn, and imposing a 20% reserve on INR derivatives (buy FX for current-account) over $2mn (FERR) and opening dedicated FX windows for OMCs
The latter provides clear direct support by moving a recurring source of dollar demand.
On FERR’s impact, around INR 600 – 700bn liquidity could be absorbed even if importer hedging reduces substantially.
Importers might shorten hedges, likely shifting dollar demand towards spot and NDFs, with net impact on forward points being ambiguous.
We believe that these measures should result in knee-jerk INR appreciation followed by some consolidation.
The package raises the near-term cost of rupee depreciation trades; it does not remove the underlying BoP pressures.
In terms of our trade recommendation, we remain long INR and IDR vs. PHP as RBI and BI are both seen as pro-FX stability central banks.

CLSA
RBI announced a slew of measures over the weekend to absorb excess liquidity and to support the Indian rupee (INR).
On Friday evening, it hiked the daily minimum cash reserve maintenance requirement from 90% to 99% (from the fortnight beginning 16 October 2026) and announced another OMO sale of Rs250bn (on 13 October 2026).
Further, like in 2013, the RBI announced a special window for OMCs to meet their daily dollar requirements.
Lastly, several FX restrictions were announced to support the INR.
All these measures should support the INR near term, possibly pushing it towards 95/US$, with further hardening of the 10-year yield and lower FX reserves.
However, after a few weeks, the discussions will likely be back to FX flows, crude oil prices and the global economic environment.
@CNBCTV18News @latha_venkatesh @_RituSingh

FY27 will not have much contribution , FY28-29 will have some real gains here for them in terms of volumes on such a useful drug , FY27 will see mostly increase in costs first and then FY28 will be monetization, they are and going themselves for selling in US rather than licensing

Key Pipeline
1) WCK 4282 (FoviscuTM)
2) WCK 4873 (Miqnaf®):
3) WCK 6777 (OdrateTM):
4) WCK 771 & WCK 2349 (Emrok® & Emrok O®)

Wockhardt 2.0 , 24-30 months runway ( this is a long game )

1) 12-18 months is breakeven /small profit , and after that topline is bottom line ( shared by management in NDTV profit interview )

2) Peak is 1.5B$ , peak is expected to have FY30-31 , trajectory acceleration, this is a long game , profits will only really show in FY28-29

Then just to see the approval document , I went to the FDA site to see how prescription of this is , Zaynich is used every 8 hours ( 3 times a day ) on the 3g medication

Prices in India will be discounted in India up to 75-80% from the US pricing

They are focusing on building a global innovator type company , post ramp up costs ,margins will be 10% higher at least at company level

Now the question is how do you play this , I think this is something crucial, I want better prices , just incase if we get a major correction in the ramp up phase due to short term cost impacts , would be very interesting to evaluate or then when the ramp up starts and we see these numbers and some early signs

But definitely an interesting company to keep tracking !

Biocon, my latest thoughts and Why things might be turning this year The elephant may be able to dance , there is a clear tactical shift in how management is talking and the re focus on aligning to the path of profitable growth that may see a comeback post a very painful last few years
Quoting the management ( Q4FY26 concall )

"We are now moving from a phase of integration and investment to one focused on execution, operating leverage and value creation. From a capital and investment perspective, the heavy lifting is largely done and behind us. Over the past few years, we have invested materially to build global scale capabilities and capacity, particularly in biosimilars, insulins, peptides and complex generics. As we stand today, this major investment phase is substantially complete. The emphasis now is on improving utilization, expanding margins and driving steady improvement in return on capital employed"

Now focusing on sweating the assets , generate cash and focus on reduction in interest costs Now how will this happen ? They have a very strong launch pipeline that is going into FY27 where H2 they may start to see tangible gains from it from an EBITDA point of view

Liraglutide Approvals in this Quarter , Yesintek ( Biosimilar to stelara which is a very expensive drug ) is also seeing increased traction across the channel Bosaya and Aukelso also launched , will keep seeing how the sales data comes why I think it is worth seeing because , Biosimilars good launches have happened , generics is improving , and they say syngene worst is over

items.title: Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue gre...
items.description_html:
Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting

Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue grew at ~55% CAGR between FY24 and FY26, while EBITDA margin expanded to ~14%, RoCE stood at ~26% and RoE at ~35%. Despite the sharp scale-up, debtor days remain relatively controlled versus several listed EPC peers.

The key monitor remains cash-flow conversion, as strong historical growth has resulted in higher receivables, retention money and working-capital requirements. However, this needs to be seen alongside the expansion in execution: the order book increased from ~₹684 crore in March 2026 to ₹916.6 crore by July 2026, while of which majority is funded bybnodal agencies like World Bank, providing relatively stronger payment visibility. The company also highlights that projects are largely supported by Central schemes and institutional financiers such as PFC, REC, ADB and the World Bank.

Importantly, Swastika is gradually moving from conventional power-distribution EPC toward more specialised and higher-value segments. It entered power transmission and renewable-energy infrastructure in 2026, while larger project credentials are expected to improve its eligibility for ₹900+ crore tenders, where management indicates competition is relatively lower. This can potentially improve both the quality and scale of the opportunity set over time.

At the IPO price band of ₹175–185, the company is valued at roughly ₹597–631 crore post-issue market capitalisation, translating to approximately 14.4x–15.2x FY26 earnings and ~1.2x FY26 revenue, based on the FY26 PAT of ₹41.4 crore. Against its historical growth, return ratios, funded order-book visibility and transition toward higher-value EPC projects, the valuation appears reasonable, with execution and working-capital conversion remaining the key factors to track.

items.description_html:
A-One Steels ~ Building A Cost-Efficient, Integrated Green Steel Platform

A-One Steels is transitioning from a regional TMT manufacturer into a more integrated steel player, focusing on backward integration, capacity expansion, product diversification and wider market reach.

Integrated Steel Value Chain: The company operates across the entire value chain — sponge iron → billets → coils → pipes/tubes → TMT, along with ferro alloys and met coke, enabling better control over raw materials and production costs.

Capacity Expansion Driving Scale: MS billet capacity has increased from 4.55 lakh MTPA in FY24 to 5.70 lakh MTPA in FY26, alongside expansion in TMT and MS pipe capacities.

Strengthening Raw Material Security: Upcoming initiatives include a 6 lakh MTPA iron ore beneficiation plant, manganese ore mining lease and a 10 MW waste heat recovery power plant to improve cost competitiveness.

New Product Opportunities: The Koppal facility provides scope to expand into products such as pellets, alloy billets and crash barriers, increasing the addressable market.

Green Energy Advantage: Around 83.2% of energy consumption is sourced from green energy, supporting lower operating costs and improving sustainability credentials.

FY26 Profitability Recovery: The company reported Rs. 4,167 Cr revenue, Rs. 304 Cr EBITDA and Rs. 127 Cr PAT in FY26, compared with EBITDA of Rs. 174 Cr and PAT of Rs. 8 Cr in FY25.

Efficient Asset Utilisation: Net fixed asset turnover stood at 6.93x in FY26, indicating strong utilisation of existing manufacturing assets.

Brand-Led Expansion: The company is strengthening its A-One Gold brand while expanding distribution reach across retail and institutional customers.

Acquisition-Led Growth Strategy: A-One Steels has historically scaled through acquisitions and continues to evaluate underutilised assets to accelerate capacity growth.

Export Readiness: CBAM compliance initiatives are underway to access European markets and tap demand for lower-carbon steel.

The Bigger Transition:
Regional Steel Manufacturer → Integrated Steel Producer → Diversified Product Platform → Pan-India & Export-Oriented Player
Key monitorables remain capacity ramp-up, leverage management (1.17x gross debt/equity), execution of backward integration projects and sustainability of FY26 profitability improvement.

items.title: Bond yields are one of the most important variables for equity markets because they effectively determine the “risk free” return available to invest...
items.description_html:
Bond yields are one of the most important variables for equity markets because they effectively determine the “risk free” return available to investors

US 10Y yield is currently ~5.25%

Why does this matter for equities?

If an investor can earn ~5.25% from a US government bond, equities need to offer a meaningfully higher expected return to justify taking additional risk

This directly impacts P/E multiples

A simple way to understand it is through the inverse of the bond yield:

At a 5.25% yield: 1 / 5.25% = ~19x

You can think of this as a rough “P/E equivalent” or inverse yield multiple for bonds
- 4% yield = ~25x
- 5% yield = ~20x
- 6% yield = ~16.7x

Now suppose a stock trades at 25x P/E

Its earnings yield is: 1 / 25 = 4%

So when a risk free government bond itself offers ~5.25%, investors naturally demand a higher return from equities

That is where the Equity Risk Premium comes in

Equities carry risk & price volatility, so investors need to be compensated for taking that additional risk

If bond yields rise while equity earnings yields remain unchanged, this risk premium gets squeezed.

The market can adjust in two ways:

Earnings rise, or stock prices fall & P/E multiples compress

Of course, equities can grow earnings over time while bond coupons generally do not, so this is not a direct apples to apples comparison

But the key point remains:

Higher bond yields raise the hurdle rate for equities

items.description_html:
NephroPlus - Key Insights from Concall

NephroPlus remained EBITDA negative for its first 11 years & PAT negative for 13 years

Dialysis has high fixed costs & does not generate attractive economics at small scale

Management quote:
“You need massive scale and you need 100% focus.”

- Q1FY27 REV grew 23.7% YoY to 282 Cr, while adj EBITDA grew ~31% to 65 Cr. EBITDA margin expanded to 23.1% from 21.9%.

- Adjusted PAT grew ~42% YoY to 37 Cr, significantly faster than REV growth. Annualised adjusted ROCE stood at ~21%.

- Underlying volumes remain healthy. Active patients grew ~13% to 38,262, while dialysis treatments increased ~13.3% to 10.3 lakh during the quarter.

- Revenue per treatment increased ~9.2% YoY to 2,733, primarily because international markets carry higher realizations. International operations now contribute ~45% of REV.

- Network expansion remains strong. NephroPlus added 26 clinics in Q1 - 19 in India & 7 in the Philippines - taking the network to 550 clinics across 357 cities & 5 countries.

- Philippines is emerging as an important validation of the India operating model. The company has reached 50 clinics across 39 cities there & become the second largest distributed dialysis network within ~6 years.

- Management continues to guide for 15-20% medium-term growth over the next 3-5 years.

- Growth is expected to come from higher utilization at existing clinics, adding clinics within existing markets, entering new countries / large PPP or M&A opportunities.

Management estimates ~80% of India's dialysis capacity is still unorganised

Management highlighted four key cost advantages behind the platform:
- Global procurement of consumables
- In house training academies for nurses & technicians
- In house biomedical maintenance capabilities
- A lean operating model developed in India's low price environment

Another interesting advantage is hospital partnerships.
Management said dialysis contributes very little to hospital economics & hospitals often lack the scale & focus to run it efficiently. NephroPlus already partners with 300+ private hospitals, allowing hospitals to save capex & operating bandwidth while continuing to earn from adjacencies such as transplants, ICU, pharmacy & diagnostics.

Working capital remains structurally high because government reimbursements typically take 3-4 months. However, receivable days improved from ~121 to ~101 day.

Management intends to add ~40-50 clinics annually in India, ~10-15 in the Philippines and target entry into a new international market every 12-18 months.

NephroPlus is evolving from an Indian dialysis chain into a global dialysis platform.

items.description_html:
Kalyan Jewellers & Titan - Strong Q2FY27

Kalyan
- Cons. REV growth: 26% YoY
- India REV & SSSG growth: ~27% & 20%
- Candere REV growth: ~64%

Another positive - non GML debt has now come down to zero

Titan
- Consumer businesses grew ~25% YoY
- Domestic business grew ~22%
- Jewellery portfolio grew ~21%

Demand remained healthy for most of the quarter, with some softening towards the end because the festive calendar shifted into Q3FY27

Studded jewellery grew in the early 30s

Buyer growth was in the mid single digits, while average ticket size increased double digits

Real test for jewellery retailers starts from H2 onwards

Over the last few quarters, a meaningful part of reported REV growth across the sector has been value led because of the sharp increase in gold prices

Simple example: If a retailer sells the same 100 grams of gold but gold prices rise 20%, reported sales value can rise ~20% even without any increase in volumes

Historically, some of the strongest earnings growth periods for jewellery retailers have come when gold prices were relatively stable. Titan is a good example.

During FY17-19, when gold prices were largely flat, Titan delivered ~25% REV CAGR & >35% EBIT CAGR. Similarly, during FY21-23, when gold prices were relatively stable, Titan delivered ~35% REV CAGR & ~60% EBIT CAGR.

When gold prices rise sharply, affordability gets impacted. Customers either postpone purchases, reduce grammage or shift towards lighter jewellery.

But once gold prices stabilise after a sharp rise, consumers gradually adjust to the new price level & buying momentum starts coming back.

That is when volume growth becomes more important.

The challenge in last 2 years was the sharp rise in gold prices, which impacted footfalls & buyer growth across the industry. If gold prices now stabilise, volumes can gradually normalise again.

items.title: RT Dhirendra Kumar: A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give invest...
items.description_html:
RT Dhirendra Kumar
A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https://vro.in/s229348. The line came from Vineet Nayar's new book, Humans First, Machines Second. His point is plain. AI is powerful and everyone has it. Something everyone has cannot make anyone special.
That left a question I did not answer. If the machine is common, what is uncommon?
I think the machine has taken the middle of the work and left us the two ends. It has not taken the beginning, which is deciding what question to ask. It has not taken the end, which is deciding whether the answer is any good.
Ask an AI to analyse a fund and you will get a competent analysis of that fund. It will not tell you that the reader's real problem is not this fund but whether he should be in this category at all. Knowing that comes from thirty years of reading letters from investors.
The machine will also give you ten sensible options. Picking the one that suits this reader in this market is not calculation. It is judgement, and judgement is mostly the memory of having been wrong before.
Then there is the story. The investor who sold everything in March 2020 did not lack information. He lacked a story strong enough to hold him when the fear came. Nobody gets that story from a prompt. AI can help you invent. It cannot invent.
One more thing. The machine agrees with you. Tell it you like a stock and it will find reasons to like it. What a person needs from an advisor or an editor is the opposite: someone willing to say no.
Nayar says the danger is not smarter machines but people losing faith in what only they can do. In our business, that is the risk worth worrying about.

items.title: I have two counter points or questions rather : - Opening a window for oil companies to take dollars from reserves is a risky bet in the circumstances...
items.description_html:
I have two counter points or questions rather :

- Opening a window for oil companies to take dollars from reserves is a risky bet in the circumstances. What if oil does not come down quickly? How long can you do this before markets start talking about whether reserves are adequate?

- In retrospect, should RBI NOT have closed the FCNR window early? We would have gotten another 50 odd billion perhaps and that would have helped if we wanted to do this arrangement eventually ?

Eventually the success/adequacy of these measures will depend on luck. if oil falls, global bond yields ease, flows return, we would have bought ourselves time to tide this period over.

If luck doesn’t favor us, perhaps we will have explore a next set of measures soon enough?

items.title: RT Tijori: Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russ...
items.description_html:
RT Tijori
Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russia Disruption

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

MRPL — exports ~40% of its output, and half its slate is diesel + ATF. Exactly what Europe will be short of.

-CPCL is an indirect beneficiary. Products transferred from CPCL to parent IOCL are billed on an import-parity pricing (IPP) basis. When international product benchmarks and cracks increase, CPCL's realized refinery-gate prices rise immediately, boosting standalone GRM and operating cash flows.

items.title: AI is carrying US markets and growth If you're worried about how much America leans on AI, look at these six numbers. (i) 42 AI stocks drove 67% of S&...
items.description_html:
AI is carrying US markets and growth

If you're worried about how much America leans on AI, look at these six numbers.

(i) 42 AI stocks drove 67% of S&P 500 returns since Jan 2024. Also 58% of earnings growth and 81% of capex growth.

(ii) The S&P sits 1% off a record. Yet about 60% of its stocks are 20% or more below their highs.

(iii) Only 30% of stocks are beating the S&P over 3 years. That's among the lowest since 1991.

(iv) AI sellers are winning, not AI users. Supply chain earnings are up 4x since March 2023. Heavy AI users are up only 30%.

(v) Tech now drives about a third of US GDP growth. In 2022, it was almost zero.

(vi) Only 20% of US states are growing faster than the national average. That's near the lowest since 1979.

Caveat: breadth was this thin in 2001. By 2003, 75% of stocks were beating the index.

items.title: 🚨 AI'S BIGGEST LOSERS COULD BE THE ONES FINANCING ITS BOOM. GS highlights four AI infrastructure business models: 🔴 Powered Shells: Predictable ...
items.description_html:
🚨 AI'S BIGGEST LOSERS COULD BE THE ONES FINANCING ITS BOOM.

GS highlights four AI infrastructure business models:

🔴 Powered Shells: Predictable revenue, low ROIC.

🟠 GPU-as-a-Service: Higher return potential, but capex-heavy and exposed to obsolescence.

🟢 Token Factories: Highest ROIC potential, but pricing and utilization risks.

🔵 Asset-Light Models: Lower capex, weaker customer lock-in.

The investor takeaway?

Don't confuse revenue growth with value creation.

A company growing 30% while earning below its cost of capital can destroy shareholder value.

The real winners won't necessarily have the biggest order books or highest capex. They'll generate the highest sustainable ROIC relative to their cost of capital.

In AI investing, follow the returns on capital, not the capex headlines.

items.title: 🚨 CHINA IS BUILDING THE AI FACTORY. WILL INDIA BE A SUPPLIER OR JUST A CUSTOMER? 🇨🇳 China's AI ecosystem spans 3,000+ companies worth nearly ...
items.description_html:
🚨 CHINA IS BUILDING THE AI FACTORY. WILL INDIA BE A SUPPLIER OR JUST A CUSTOMER?

🇨🇳 China's AI ecosystem spans 3,000+ companies worth nearly $10 TRILLION.

But here's the surprise: AI models account for just $300 billion.

GS' AI value-chain mapping reveals where the real industrial opportunity lies:

🔹 Semiconductors: $2.6T
🔹 Power & Energy: $1.4T
🔹 AI Infrastructure: $1.0T
🔹 AI Models: $300B
🔹 AI Applications: $2.3T

China isn't just building smarter AI. It's building the factories, chips, power grids and infrastructure that make AI possible.

🇮🇳 India needs to think beyond AI apps and IT services.

Our opportunity lies in power equipment, data centres, semiconductor packaging, cooling systems, industrial automation and specialised AI products.

We should aim to BUILD infrastructure, OWN intellectual property and EXPORT technology.

Otherwise, India risks becoming a massive AI consumer while much of the economic value flows overseas.

In the last technology cycle, India exported talent and services. In this AI cycle, can we export technology, equipment and intellectual property?

That's the difference between participating in a revolution and owning a piece of it.

China is building the AI factory. India must decide whether to supply the world or simply buy from it.
